content: Dementia is formally recognized within a ministry portfolio as a condition that is actively monitored, with a government department or agency responsible for its oversight. This recognition ensures that dementia is included in national health and social care strategies, policies, and plans, enabling a comprehensive response to the condition. To gather relevant data on dementia, it may be necessary to proactively contact key personnel across various institutions, agencies, and facilities within your country. These personnel may include stakeholders from the health and social care sectors, as well as those from education, academia, and civil society. A list of potential data sources is provided for each indicator in the reference guide, but the relevance of these sources may vary depending on the organization of your country’s health and social care systems. It is essential to use all relevant data sources to provide the most comprehensive feedback. If alternative data sources are used, this information should be included in the comment box provided for the specific indicator. Examples of national bodies that can be contacted for data include: The National Health Information System for data on health facilities and human resources. The financial department of the Ministry of Health for data on government spending. The Ministry of Social Affairs for data on social services available to people with dementia and their caregivers. Professional institutes and other bodies for data on human resources, guidelines, and training programs. It is recommended to first identify data at the national level (central government) and then at subnational levels (e.g., provinces, states, districts, or facilities). Some data may already be compiled, while other data may require aggregation from various sources. If your response to a measure only partially addresses the question or includes caveats, select the response that best corresponds to your country’s setting. Additional information can be entered in the e-tool’s comment field associated with a specific indicator or in the log section at the end of the tool. If the definition of dementia in the glossary differs from the one commonly used in your country, use the definition provided in the glossary. If reconciliation is not possible, state this in the e-tool’s comment field or log field. To reduce the burden of data collection, the World Health Organization (WHO) collaborates with international partners and links to international databases for data already collected, such as WHO’s Global Health Observatory, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), and the European Union’s Joint Programme on Neurodegenerative Disease Research (JPND). Relevant indicators are marked with an asterisk to indicate that data might already be available. If your country provides data to other international organizations on measures relevant to the Global Dementia Observatory (GDO) but not marked, indicate this in the e-tool’s comment field. Dementia requires a broad public health approach involving the entire government and multiple stakeholders to develop a comprehensive response from the health and social care systems (both public and private) and other government sectors. The development and coordination of policies, strategies, plans, and integrated dementia programs through a multisectoral approach will support the recognition of the complex needs of people with dementia and address those needs within the context of each country. The inclusion of people with dementia and their caregivers, along with other relevant stakeholders and partners, is crucial for the success and acceptance of this process. Setting up a focal point, unit, or functional sector responsible for dementia or a coordination mechanism for dementia will facilitate the coordination of a comprehensive, all-of-government, multisectoral response to dementia. This includes the existence of a focal point, unit, sector, or other body within the Ministry of Health (or equivalent) responsible for dementia. The development and coordination of policies, strategies, plans, or frameworks through a comprehensive, multisectoral approach will support the recognition of people with dementia and address their complex needs and rights within the context of each country. A written or organized set of principles, objectives, or actions for reducing the burden attributable to dementia in a population is considered valid if it has been approved or published by the Ministry of Health (or equivalent) or parliament. The dementia plan should include funding to operationalize the latest dementia-specific national policy, strategy, plan, or framework. Funding allocation should be referenced in the budget of the most recently published policy, strategy, plan, or framework document. The plan should also include targets or milestones for monitoring implementation during the operational phase. Dementia may also be integrated into or covered by other national plans, such as mental health, aging, non-communicable diseases (NCDs), or disability policies, strategies, plans, or frameworks. These are considered valid if they have been approved or published by the Ministry of Health (or equivalent) or parliament. A subnational dementia-specific policy, strategy, plan, or framework will be assessed as “operational” if it is used and implemented in the country, has funds and resources, and is being monitored or evaluated for implementation. The percentage of states or provinces covered by comprehensive subnational dementia-specific policies, strategies, plans, or frameworks should also be assessed. The dementia plan should align with cross-cutting principles outlined in the global action plan on the public health response to dementia (2017–2025). These principles include: A human rights-based approach that is sensitive to the needs, expectations, and rights of people with dementia, consistent with international human rights instruments. Equity, supporting gender equity and a gender-sensitive perspective, while addressing vulnerabilities specific to each national context. Empowerment of people with dementia, their caregivers, and families, involving them in advocacy, policy, planning, legislation, service provision, monitoring, and research. Multisectoral collaboration, encouraging partnerships among all stakeholders to improve prevention, risk reduction, diagnosis, treatment, and care. Support for universal health coverage, ensuring equitable access to a broad range of services for people with dementia and their caregivers. The dementia plan should also address specific action areas, such as: Dementia awareness, stigma reduction, and dementia-friendly communities tailored to cultural contexts and community needs. Dementia prevention and risk reduction, linking dementia with other programs and promoting evidence-based interventions. Timely dementia diagnosis, post-diagnostic supports, and care, including sustainable care systems across the continuum from diagnosis to end-of-life care. Workforce training on dementia, building the knowledge and skills of health professionals to deliver evidence-based, culturally appropriate, and human rights-sensitive care.
